questions.question: Define reaction rate and activation energy. Then use collision theory to explain, separately, why grinding a solid reactant to powder and why raising the temperature each increase the rate of a reaction — making clear which mechanism dominates in each case.
questions.expected_answer: Reaction rate is the change in the concentration or amount of reactants or products per unit time (units mol·s⁻¹ or mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹). Activation energy is the minimum kinetic energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur. Collision theory: particles react only through effective collisions — collisions with correct orientation and with energy at least equal to the activation energy — so rate is set by the number of effective collisions per second. Grinding to powder: only particles at a surface can be struck; powdering exposes vastly more particles, so the frequency of collisions rises and with it the number of effective collisions per second — this works by increasing collision frequency, not the success fraction. Raising temperature: particles gain average kinetic energy, so a much larger fraction of collisions carries at least the activation energy; collision frequency also rises slightly, but the dominant mechanism is the larger fraction of successful collisions, which is why temperature is the most powerful rate factor.

questions.question: Equal masses of powdered magnesium and magnesium ribbon are added to separate flasks of the same excess dilute acid, and the hydrogen volume is logged against time. Sketch-describe the two curves, explaining why they start differently but flatten at the same height, and state what a LOWER plateau in one flask would have implied.
questions.expected_answer: Both curves rise from the origin, climb steeply at first, bend over as reactant is consumed, and end horizontal. The powder's curve is much steeper initially: its far greater exposed surface area allows more collisions per second between acid particles and magnesium, so more effective collisions per second and a faster rate. The ribbon's curve rises more gently. However, equal masses of magnesium contain equal moles, and with acid in excess both must eventually release the same moles of hydrogen — so both curves flatten at the same final volume: the rate changed but the extent did not. If one curve had flattened at a lower plateau, that run must have had a different amount of available reactant — less magnesium, or the acid limiting — because plateau height measures extent, not speed.

questions.question: Using the molecular energy distribution curve, explain how (a) raising the temperature and (b) adding a catalyst each increase reaction rate, stating clearly which feature of the diagram changes in each case, and why a catalyst leaves ΔH unchanged.
questions.expected_answer: The distribution curve plots number of particles against kinetic energy; only particles to the right of the activation energy line can collide effectively. (a) Raising temperature: the curve itself shifts toward higher energies and flattens, with total area unchanged since the number of particles is unchanged; the tail beyond the activation energy line grows substantially, so a much larger fraction of collisions is effective and the rate rises — the CURVE moves, the line stays. (b) Adding a catalyst: the curve does not move at all; instead the catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so the activation energy LINE moves left and many more of the existing particles already lie beyond the new threshold — the LINE moves, the curve stays. On the potential-energy diagram the catalyst lowers only the hump between reactants and products; the energies of the reactants and products themselves are untouched, so ΔH — the difference between those two levels — is exactly the same. The catalyst is also not consumed by the reaction.
